title: Sonos Speakers for Home Theater (2026): Best Setups, Ranked
metaDescription: The best Sonos setup for 1 small room is Beam (Gen 2) plus Sub 4; living rooms get Arc Ultra plus 2 Era 100s, big rooms 2 Era 300s. Builds with room maths.
keywords: best sonos setup for home theater
best setup for sonos home theater
what is the best sonos setup for home theater
best sonos speakers for home theater
intro:
The best Sonos home theater setup for most living rooms is the [Sonos Arc Ultra](/gear/sonos-arc-ultra/) with a pair of [Era 100](/gear/sonos-era-100/) speakers as surrounds, then a [Sub 4](/gear/sonos-sub-4/) when you are ready for deeper bass. This guide is for anyone who wants Sonos's wireless, app-driven approach and needs to know which combination to buy for their room and budget.

We break Sonos into three tiers, from a compact Beam-based system to the full Arc Ultra, Sub 4 and Era 300 build, and show the room maths behind each. Rankings are built on Sonos's spec sheets and owner reports. One honest warning up front: Sonos does not decode DTS:X, and every tier costs more than a comparable Samsung all-in-one.
quickAnswer: The best Sonos home theater setup depends on room size. Small rooms: Beam (Gen 2) plus Sub 4. Medium living rooms: Arc Ultra plus two Era 100s as surrounds. Large rooms and film fans: Arc Ultra, Sub 4 and two Era 300s, which adds rear height effects for full Dolby Atmos. Buy the soundbar first, then add whichever piece fixes your biggest gap.

picks.body:
**Why it wins:** The Arc Ultra is the heart of the two best Sonos setups. Sonos lists **14 drivers** and describes it as a **9.1.4** system on its own, with up-firing drivers for [Dolby Atmos](/glossary/dolby-atmos/) height effects and a new Sound Motion woofer that Sonos claims delivers up to double the bass of the original Arc. That matters because it is the first Sonos bar where skipping the sub at first is a reasonable plan.

It is about **46 inches wide**. A 55-inch TV is roughly 48 inches wide and a 65-inch about 57 inches, so the Arc Ultra suits 55-inch screens and up. Smaller TVs make it look oversized.

You get [HDMI eARC](/glossary/earc/), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay 2, Speech Enhancement and Trueplay [room correction](/glossary/room-correction/), including a Quick Tune mode that uses the bar's own microphones, so Android owners can calibrate too.

**The trade-off:** no DTS:X decoding and only one HDMI port, so all sources go through your TV. There is no optical input either; older TVs need Sonos's adapter.

**Who it suits:** medium and large living rooms, and anyone planning to grow into the full system. Against the [Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar](/gear/bose-smart-ultra-soundbar/), it has more drivers and the far stronger multiroom platform; Bose counters with a better dialogue mode and an optical input.

**Why it wins:** The Beam (Gen 2) is the entry point for a Sonos home theater, in the **$400–$500** band. It packs **five drivers** (four woofers and a tweeter) plus passive radiators into a cabinet about **26 inches wide**, which suits TVs from about 43 to 55 inches. It decodes Dolby Atmos, but there are no up-firing drivers: height effects are virtual, created with processing rather than sound bounced off the ceiling.

That is fine in a bedroom or small lounge where you sit close. Owners report clear dialogue, strong Speech Enhancement and a surprisingly wide soundstage for the size. HDMI eARC and Sonos's full app and multiroom features are included.

**The trade-off:** bass. A 26-inch bar cannot produce deep low end, and it runs out of headroom in larger rooms. That is why our small-room tier pairs it with a sub rather than surrounds.

**Who it suits:** rooms under roughly 2,000 cubic feet and TVs up to 55 inches. It is also the best way into Sonos if you already own Sonos speakers for music. Compared with the Arc Ultra above, you give up nine drivers, real up-firing Atmos and a lot of bass, but you save more than half. Against the [Bose Smart Soundbar](/gear/bose-smart-soundbar/), it is a close match on size and price; pick Sonos for multiroom, Bose for its dialogue mode.

**Why it wins:** The Sub 4 is Sonos's full-size wireless subwoofer, and for movies it is the biggest upgrade you can make to either soundbar. It keeps Sonos's force-cancelling layout, with two drivers facing each other inside the cabinet so their vibrations cancel out, which means less cabinet rattle and the freedom to stand it upright or lay it flat under a sofa. Its slot design lets sound escape through the center opening.

Pairing takes a minute in the app. Once connected, the bar stops trying to reproduce the lowest frequencies, which also gives dialogue and mid-bass more headroom at higher volumes.

**The maths problem:** Sonos does not publish a driver size, amplifier wattage or frequency response for the Sub 4. In the **$700–$800** band, a passive 12-inch sub from SVS publishes all three, but Sonos bars have no standard subwoofer output, so only Sonos subs work. Sonos does let the Arc Ultra run two subs in large rooms.

**The trade-off:** it often costs more than the Beam it is paired with. In small rooms, Sonos's cheaper Sub Mini (not ranked here) is worth a look.

**Who it suits:** anyone who watches action films, especially with the Arc Ultra in a medium or large room. In our top tier it is not optional: an Arc Ultra with Era 300s but no sub sounds light against the scale of the rest of the system.

picks.award: Best Sonos Surrounds for Dolby Atmos
picks.body:
**Why it wins:** The Era 300 is the only Sonos speaker built for spatial audio, and as rear surrounds it completes the most capable Sonos home theater. Each one has **six drivers**: four tweeters (including one that fires upward and one forward) and two side-firing woofers. Paired with the Arc Ultra as surrounds, they add rear height effects, so overhead sounds can move from front to back as well as side to side.

This is the difference between "Atmos from the front" and a full dome of sound. Owners moving from Era 100 surrounds to Era 300s consistently describe a bigger, more enveloping rear soundstage, especially with Atmos films.

**The trade-off:** size and price. Each Era 300 is a large, oddly shaped speaker, and a pair costs roughly what the Arc Ultra does. They also need stands or sturdy shelves at about ear height with clear space above for the up-firing driver.

**Who it suits:** film fans in medium or large rooms who already own an Arc Ultra and Sub 4. If you only want surround effects behind you rather than overhead, the Era 100 below gives you most of the benefit for around half the cost.

**Why it wins:** The Era 100 is the smart-money surround for a Sonos system. Each speaker has **two angled tweeters and a woofer**, and on its own it plays in stereo. As a pair of rear surrounds, each Era 100 handles one surround channel, giving you a proper 5.0 setup with an Arc Ultra or Beam, or 5.1 once a sub is added.

In the **$200–$250** band per speaker, a pair costs about half as much as two Era 300s. That is why our middle tier pairs the Arc Ultra with Era 100s: in a typical living room, getting sound behind you is a bigger jump than adding rear height channels.

It also works as a kitchen or office speaker the rest of the time, with Bluetooth and a USB-C line-in through an adapter, so the purchase is not wasted if you later move up to Era 300s.

**The trade-off:** no up-firing driver, so no rear height effects. Front height still comes from the Arc Ultra.

**Who it suits:** medium living rooms where the sofa is within a few feet of a wall or side table to place the speakers on. Compared with the Era 300 above, you lose overhead effects at the back but keep convincing side and rear surround. It is a much smaller box, which matters if your seating is against a wall.

sections.heading: The Short Verdict
sections.body:
Sonos is the best-integrated wireless home theater you can buy if you also want whole-home music. Everything pairs through one app, setups grow one speaker at a time, and resale values stay strong. Here are the three tiers we recommend:

| Tier | Setup | Best for | Approx. price band |
|---|---|---|---|
| Starter | Beam (Gen 2) + Sub 4 | Small rooms, TVs up to 55 in | $1,200–$1,300 |
| Middle | Arc Ultra + two Era 100s | Medium living rooms | $1,350–$1,500 |
| Full | Arc Ultra + Sub 4 + two Era 300s | Large rooms, film fans | $2,500–$2,800 |

The weak spots are price and formats. Sonos does not decode DTS:X, and the full system costs about what a [Samsung HW-Q990F](/gear/samsung-hw-q990f/) and a good [receiver](/best-home-theater-receiver/) would together. If you only care about movies, there is more sound per dollar elsewhere. If you want a system the whole family can run from their phones, Sonos is the one to beat.

sections.heading: Who Sonos Is
sections.body:
Sonos was founded in 2002 in Santa Barbara, California, and invented the mainstream wireless multiroom speaker. Its home theater range grew from the original Playbar into today's lineup of soundbars ([Arc Ultra](/gear/sonos-arc-ultra/), [Beam (Gen 2)](/gear/sonos-beam-gen-2/) and the smaller Ray), subwoofers ([Sub 4](/gear/sonos-sub-4/) and Sub Mini) and speakers that double as surrounds ([Era 100](/gear/sonos-era-100/) and [Era 300](/gear/sonos-era-300/)).

Every Sonos product runs on the same Wi-Fi platform. That means any speaker in your house can play the TV audio, the surrounds can be moved to the kitchen for a party, and the system updates itself. It also means everything depends on the Sonos app. In 2024 Sonos released a redesigned app that owners widely reported as buggy and missing features; the company has since issued many fixes and publicly apologized, but it is fair to factor that history in.

Sonos is a closed system: Sonos bars only pair with Sonos subs and surrounds, and there is no way to add a passive subwoofer or speaker. See the full range on our [Sonos brand page](/brands/sonos/).

sections.heading: The Best Sonos Home Theater Setup at Every Budget
sections.body:
The best Sonos home theater setup is the one that fixes your room's biggest problem first. Here is how each tier earns its place, with room volume as the guide (length x width x height in feet).

**Starter: Beam (Gen 2) + Sub 4.** For rooms under about 2,000 cubic feet, such as 12 x 15 x 8 ft (1,440 cu ft). In a small room you sit close to the bar, so virtual Atmos works reasonably well, and the Beam's weakness is bass, not width. Adding the [Sub 4](/gear/sonos-sub-4/) fixes that. If budget is tight, the Sub Mini does the same job at lower output.

**Middle: Arc Ultra + two Era 100s.** For rooms of about 2,000 to 3,500 cubic feet, such as 16 x 18 x 9 ft (2,592 cu ft). The [Arc Ultra](/gear/sonos-arc-ultra/) has enough bass on its own to sound full in a medium room, so the bigger gap is the lack of sound behind you. Two [Era 100s](/gear/sonos-era-100/) give you real rear surround channels. Add the Sub 4 later.

**Full: Arc Ultra + Sub 4 + two Era 300s.** For rooms over about 3,000 cubic feet or open-plan spaces, and for anyone who watches a lot of Atmos films. The [Era 300s](/gear/sonos-era-300/) add rear height channels, and the Sub 4 provides the low end the scale of this system needs. In very large rooms, the Arc Ultra can take a second Sub 4.

A simple upgrade path: buy the Arc Ultra, add Era 100s, add a Sub 4, and if you still want more, move the Era 100s to another room and add Era 300s at the back. Nothing you buy gets wasted.

For how an Arc Ultra system compares with the Samsung HW-Q990F and receiver-based speaker packages, see our [best home theater system](/best-home-theater-systems/) rankings, where it is our Best Soundbar-Based System.

sections.heading: Setup and Placement Tips
sections.body:
- **Bar position.** Center the bar under the screen with the front edge flush with the TV stand. Do not tuck it inside a cabinet; the Arc Ultra's up-firing drivers need a clear path to the ceiling. Flat ceilings of about 8 to 10 feet work best for reflected height effects.
- **Surround placement.** Put Era 100s or Era 300s slightly behind and to the sides of your main seat, at about ear height. Keep them within roughly the same distance from the seat; Trueplay can correct small differences.
- **Sub placement.** Start the Sub 4 at the front of the room near a wall, then try alternative spots. Corners boost output but can make bass boomy. Because it is wireless, moving it only needs a power outlet.
- **Run Trueplay after every change.** Calibrate again each time you add or move a speaker. Arc Ultra's Quick Tune uses the bar's own microphones; the more detailed walk-around tuning uses your phone.
- **Check your TV's audio output.** Set it to eARC or passthrough so Dolby Atmos reaches the bar. Use our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/) to check your seating position at the same time.
- **Use wired Ethernet for the bar if you can.** Sonos systems are more stable with a solid network connection, especially with four or five speakers in the group.

sections.heading: What Sonos Does Well
sections.body:
**Expandability.** You can start with one bar and add surrounds, a sub or a second sub over time, and every piece has a second life as a music speaker.

**Multiroom.** No other home theater system makes it this easy to play the TV in the kitchen, group speakers for a party or stream music to every room.

**Dialogue and night modes.** Speech Enhancement and Night Sound are easy to toggle from the app or your TV remote, and owners report both work well.

**Atmos from a single bar.** The Arc Ultra's up-firing drivers produce real height effects without extra speakers, and Sonos calls it 9.1.4 on its own.

**Resale.** Sonos gear holds its value well on the used market.

sections.heading: Where Sonos Falls Short
sections.body:
**No DTS:X.** Sonos plays Dolby Atmos and standard DTS, but not DTS:X. Many 4K Blu-rays use DTS:X, so disc collectors lose the object-based version.

**One HDMI port.** There is no HDMI passthrough, so every source plugs into the TV and relies on the TV passing Atmos over [eARC](/glossary/earc/).

**Cost of the full build.** The top tier lands at around $2,500–$2,800. A [Samsung HW-Q990F](/gear/samsung-hw-q990f/) with 11.1.4 channels, DTS:X, sub and up-firing rears costs less. A passive [Klipsch](/klipsch-home-theater-review/) or [Polk](/polk-audio-review/) system with a receiver plays louder for less.

**Few published specs.** Sonos does not publish wattage or driver sizes for the Sub 4, so you cannot compare output.

**App dependence.** The 2024 app problems showed the risk of a system that runs entirely on software. Things are much improved, but you are trusting Sonos to keep it that way.

**Closed system.** No subwoofer output, no speaker terminals, no way to add a passive sub. You are in the Sonos world for good.

sections.heading: Sonos vs Bose, Samsung and Sony
sections.body:
| | Sonos | Bose | Samsung | Sony |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Top bar | Arc Ultra | Smart Ultra Soundbar | HW-Q990F (system) | Bravia Theater Bar 9 |
| DTS:X | No | No | Yes | Yes |
| Calibration | Trueplay | ADAPTiQ | SpaceFit Sound Pro | Sound Field Optimization |
| TV-brand perks | None | None | Q-Symphony | Acoustic Center Sync |
| Multiroom | Best in class | Good | Limited | Limited |

**Sonos vs Bose:** the closest rival. Bose's dialogue mode is better and its bars keep an optical input; Sonos has more speaker options, dual-sub support and much stronger multiroom. Read our [Bose home theater review](/bose-home-theater-review/).

**Sonos vs Samsung:** the [Samsung HW-Q990F](/gear/samsung-hw-q990f/) gives you a complete 11.1.4 system in one box with DTS:X for less than the full Sonos build, and it adds Q-Symphony with Samsung TVs. Sonos wins on flexibility and music. See our [Samsung home theater review](/samsung-home-theater-review/).

**Sonos vs Sony:** Sony's [Bravia Theater Bar 9](/gear/sony-bravia-theater-bar-9/) decodes DTS:X and links to Bravia TVs through Acoustic Center Sync. If you own a recent Bravia, compare it closely. See our [Sony home theater review](/sony-home-theater-review/).

sections.heading: How We Chose These Setups
sections.body:
We started from the three combinations Sonos buyers ask about most, then checked each against room volume, TV width and cost. Product rankings reflect what each piece adds to a real living room, based on Sonos's published specs and owner-reported reliability.

The Arc Ultra ranks first because it anchors two of the three tiers. The Beam ranks second as the only sensible small-room bar. The Sub 4 ranks above the surrounds because it improves every film, not only surround mixes. Between the surrounds, the Era 300 ranks higher for capability, but the Era 100 earns its place as the better value for most living rooms. We left out the Ray because its lack of HDMI makes it a TV speaker upgrade rather than a home theater foundation.

sections.heading: Who Should Skip Sonos
sections.body:
- **DTS:X disc collectors.** Choose Samsung, Sony or an AV receiver.
- **Value-first movie fans.** A [budget home theater system](/best-budget-home-theater-system/) or a receiver with passive [home theater speakers](/best-home-theater-speakers/) gives you more output per dollar.
- **Anyone who wants a passive subwoofer.** Sonos has no sub output. If deep, measured bass matters, see our [subwoofer guide](/best-subwoofer-for-home-theater/).
- **People who dislike app-only control.** Sonos expects you to use the app for setup, calibration and grouping.

Weighing other cable-free options? See our [best wireless home theater system](/best-wireless-home-theater-system/) guide.

Sonos bar silent? Work through the [soundbar no-sound fixes for HDMI ARC and eARC](/soundbar-no-sound-hdmi-arc-earc/). Buying in the holiday sales? See the [Cyber Monday soundbar price targets](/cyber-monday-soundbar-deals/).

mistakes.title: Buying the Arc Ultra for a small TV
mistakes.body: At about 46 inches wide, the Arc Ultra overhangs anything smaller than a 50-inch TV. For 43 to 50-inch screens, the Beam (Gen 2) looks and fits better and costs far less.

mistakes.title: Hiding the bar in a cabinet
mistakes.body: The Arc Ultra's up-firing drivers bounce sound off the ceiling. Put it inside a TV unit or under a shelf and you lose most of the height effect you paid for.

mistakes.title: Skipping Trueplay
mistakes.body: Trueplay adjusts each speaker for your room. Owners who skip it often report boomy bass and quiet surrounds. Run it again whenever you add or move a speaker.

mistakes.title: Pairing a cheap sub with a big room
mistakes.body: The Sub Mini is designed for small to medium rooms. In a large open-plan space it runs out of headroom; choose the Sub 4, or two Sub 4s with the Arc Ultra.

mistakes.title: Expecting DTS:X from discs
mistakes.body: Sonos does not decode DTS:X. If most of your Blu-rays use it, buy a system that does, or accept that you will hear a downmixed version.

faqs.q: What is the best Sonos setup for home theater?
faqs.a: For most living rooms, the best Sonos setup for home theater is the Arc Ultra with two Era 100s as rear surrounds, adding a Sub 4 later. Small rooms do well with the Beam (Gen 2) and Sub 4. Large rooms and film fans should go for the Arc Ultra, Sub 4 and two Era 300s for full Dolby Atmos.

faqs.q: Is a Sonos sub worth it for home theater?
faqs.a: Yes, for movies. A Sonos sub takes the lowest frequencies off the soundbar, which adds weight to effects and frees the bar to play dialogue more cleanly at higher volumes. The Sub 4 suits medium and large rooms; the Sub Mini is enough for small rooms. With music-only use, it is less essential.

faqs.q: Should I add surrounds or a sub first?
faqs.a: It depends on the bar. With the Beam (Gen 2), add the sub first, because bass is its biggest weakness. With the Arc Ultra, which has much stronger bass, surrounds usually add more first in a medium room. Film fans in large rooms will want both eventually.

faqs.q: Can I use Era speakers as Sonos surrounds?
faqs.a: Yes. Both the Era 100 and Era 300 can be paired as rear surrounds with Sonos soundbars. Era 100s give you standard rear surround channels. Era 300s add rear height channels with the Arc Ultra, creating a fuller Dolby Atmos effect. The pair must be the same model.

No. Sonos soundbars support Dolby Atmos, Dolby TrueHD and standard DTS, but they do not decode DTS:X. If your Blu-ray player sends DTS:X, you will hear a non-object version. Samsung's HW-Q990F, Sony's Bravia Theater bars and AV receivers do decode DTS:X.

faqs.q: Is Sonos better than Bose for home theater?
faqs.a: Sonos is better for expandability and multiroom music, with more speaker options and support for two subs on the Arc Ultra. Bose is better for dialogue clarity and has an optical input. Neither decodes DTS:X. If you want a whole-home system, choose Sonos; if speech clarity is the priority, choose Bose.

faqs.q: Do Sonos surround speakers need to be plugged in?
faqs.a: Yes. Sonos surrounds connect to the soundbar wirelessly, but every Era speaker and every Sonos sub needs its own power outlet. Plan outlet locations near your seating before buying, especially if the sofa is in the middle of the room.

bottomLine: The best Sonos home theater setup for most homes is the [Arc Ultra](/gear/sonos-arc-ultra/) with two [Era 100s](/gear/sonos-era-100/), adding a [Sub 4](/gear/sonos-sub-4/) when budget allows. Small rooms should start with the [Beam (Gen 2)](/gear/sonos-beam-gen-2/) and a sub, and film fans with big rooms should finish with [Era 300s](/gear/sonos-era-300/) for full Dolby Atmos. Sonos is not the cheapest way to get surround sound and it skips DTS:X, but no rival matches how easily it grows, moves between rooms and doubles as a whole-home music system.
